title: The senior says leave him at home
stem:
You are an F2 doctor on an out-of-hours home visit. Mr Lowe, 82, lives alone and has a chest infection. He is newly confused, his respiratory rate is 26, and his oxygen saturation is 91% on air.

You phone the senior GP at base, who advises starting oral antibiotics and leaving him at home. You think he needs admission.
instruction: Choose the 3 most appropriate actions to take in this situation.

options.text: Leave him at home with oral antibiotics, as the senior GP has advised you to.
options.brief: Doesn't act on your concerns about a sick patient.
options.detailed: The senior's advice deserves respect, but you have seen him and are concerned. Accepting advice you think is unsafe, without discussing it further, isn't appropriate.

options.text: Ask a neighbour to check on him overnight.
options.brief: Not a substitute for appropriate medical care.
options.detailed: A neighbour may help, but he may need oxygen and hospital treatment.

options.text: Call 999 for an emergency ambulance yourself.
options.brief: May be needed in an emergency, but bypasses the senior.
options.detailed: If he deteriorated rapidly, an emergency ambulance would be right. But he is stable enough for a discussion, and the senior should know.

options.text: Repeat your specific findings to the senior GP.
options.brief: The senior may not have taken in how unwell he is.
options.detailed: New confusion, a raised respiratory rate and low oxygen saturation are concerning, especially in an older person living alone. Repeating them clearly may change the advice.

options.text: Tell the senior GP you'd like to refer him to the medical team.
options.brief: Open escalation is appropriate when you remain concerned.
options.detailed: If you still believe he needs admission, saying so openly and proposing a referral is professional and keeps the senior informed.

options.text: Tell Mr Lowe the senior GP is wrong.
options.brief: Undermines a colleague and doesn't help him.
options.detailed: He needs a plan, not to be drawn into a disagreement between doctors.

options.text: Document your findings and the advice you were given.
options.brief: A clear record supports any decision.
options.detailed: Recording your findings, the advice, and the decision reached protects Mr Lowe and you.

options.text: Start antibiotics and arrange a visit for tomorrow morning.
options.brief: May be too late if he deteriorates overnight.
options.detailed: This is a reasonable plan for a less unwell patient, but his observations suggest he may deteriorate before then.

explanation.issue: This tests how you escalate a concern when a senior's advice, given by phone, differs from your own assessment.
explanation.keyDetails: His observations are abnormal. He is confused and lives alone. The senior hasn't seen him.
explanation.reasoning: [D] gives the senior the full picture, [E] escalates openly, and [G] records it. The distractors accept advice you think is unsafe ([A], [H]), rely on others ([B]), bypass the senior ([C]), or undermine them ([F]).
explanation.competing: [H] is the hard distractor: it's reasonable for a less unwell patient, but his observations suggest he needs more.

references.title: Good medical practice
references.note: Domain 3, escalating concerns about patient safety.
